speakeroldname: Hon. W. R. MOTHERWELL (Minister of Agriculture):
speechtext:
The act under which these
grants are made was passed in 1907, and the money is paid on the basis of thirty per cent of the cost of construction. That sum is given by way of subsidy, conditional upon supervision of plans, construction and so on. The grant extends over four or five payments. The provisions of the act were pretty generally taken advantage of for a number of years although during the war activities were suspended to some extent owing to the fact that the act was made applicable only to municipal cold storages. Since this government came into power, however, it has again been made applicable to cold storages generally. The demand for subsidies has somewhat fallen off recently, the feeling being that Canada is fairly well supplied with facilities in this direction. For that reason the vote has been reduced.

The vote
covers only the grants?
Yes, and the money is all for contracts already entered into. The contract which will take most of the grant is located in Sydney, Cape Breton.

How
many of these plants have been subsidized and what total has been spent to date?

These plants extend over the whole Dominion, from Prince Rupert to Halifax. The number of plants and the total expended in the various provinces are, in round numbers:
Province	Total expenditure
Prince Edward Island, 2	 $ 20,000
Nova Scotia, 4	 142,000
New Brunswick,	2	 57,000
Quebec, 4	(approximately) 85,000
Ontario, 16	 183,000
Manitoba, 1	 9.000
Saskatchewan, 4	 80,000
Alberta, 2	 72,000
British Columbia, 3	 137,000
The total number of plants receiving assistance is thirty-eight, and the total subsidy paid, $795,000.

How
many of the plants which have been in operation are now out of business?
They are all operating.
Where are the two plants in New Brunswick located, and when were the grants given them?

While my deputy
is looking up that information I may anticipate a question which will likely be asked in reference to Halifax. I have had a number of communications from hon. members from Nova Scotia and I may point out here that this vote is not sufficient to take care of the project which they have in view for Halifax. From what I can gather from the correspondence I have had with hon. members, including my hon. friend from Halifax (Mr. Black), I think that what they have in mind is something substantial, not perhaps as large as the establishment at Montreal, but a plant which will be handled by the harbour board, if there is such an institution in Halifax. Obviously this vote could not meet the requirements of a large port enterprise such as the one we have at Montreal.

At what point in Nova
Scotia are the plants operating?

Certain large enterprises do not come under this vote, and I referred to Halifax merely to point out that any considerable project which might be anticipated there could not be taken care of by such a vote as this.

Harbour proposals do not
come under this vote?
No.
How much was spent of last year's estimate of $70,000?
About *30,000 in round figures, to meet payments on contracts already entered into.

What explains
the decrease?

We	usually have
certain votes in the supplementaries. After the House has met and spring comes and we have a fair idea of the prospect of the fruit crop we generally include a vote in the supplementary estimates for fruit-cooling establishments which have been receiving assistance in British Columbia. The extra $40,000 was in the supplementaries last year.
Replying to the hon. member for York-Sunbury, the cold storage plants in New Brunswick are located as follows: the New Brunswick Cold Storage Company, at St. John, total subsidy granted, $50,100; Imperial Products Company, Limited, Woodstock, subsidy granted, $7,673.

Do I understand the minister to say that none of this supplementary estimate was spent?

Supply-Agriculture
Practically none.

The minister
admits that he brought down a supplementary estimate at the end of the session and did not spend any of it?

Yes. It was thought that a number of the fruit districts would be able to enter into this co-operative plan, but on account of the bad fruit season they were unable to do so. In British Columbia-I have particular reference to the vicinity of Nelson-the fruit men there expected to be able to raise their part of the expenditure, because it must be remembered that this amount represents only thirty per cent of the expenditure, the fruit growers putting up the other seventy per cent, but after the estimates were passed it was found that the fruit growers at Nelson and elsewhere were not able to take advantage of it because of the poor fruit crop of last year, due to the previous bad winter season, which affected the trees very adversely. In the town of Vernon we could have expended some money, but their fruit crop was also away off in quantity, and there was also some difference of opinion between the town of Vernon and Kelowna as to which should get assistance. Strong representations were made to us from Kelowna that we should supplement what we had already given them the year before, which was $20,000, for an addition to their packing plant and pre-cooling facilities, but there was a difference of opinion between them and the fruit men who had made the representations in the first instance, and the result was that the money was not expended in either place. I have been in correspondence with the member for Yale (Mr. Stirling) who has taken an active interest in this matter, and I have assured him that after the spring season has opened and we have a fair idea of what the fruit prospects will be, it is quite possible that we may have to add to this a little in the sup-plementaries to take care of a possible expenditure in either Kelowna or Vernon.

Did the minister say the
federal government paid 30 or 15 per cent?
Thirty per cent.

Did it not use to be 15 per
cent?

No, it was always
30 per cent.
The Auditor General's report speaks as though in 1924-1925 it was 15 per cent.	I
It is spread out in instalments, the first payment being 15 per cent, and then so much more as the work proceeds.
I notice that these estimates were always under the title "Arts and Agriculture" up until the regime of the present minister. May I ask him how he succeeded in getting rdd of the "Arts"?
We tried to preserve the art of getting the estimates through. I really do not know the story, Mr. Chairman.
Will the minister say where these plants are situated in Nova Scotia?

Lockeport Cold
Storage, total subsidy, in round figures, $17,000; Halifax Cold Storage Company, at Port Hawkesbury, $9,000; St. Leonard Fisheries, Limited, formerly called the North Atlantic Fisheries, $60,000. Then there is one in Cape Breton, at North Sydney, where the amount was $36,000.
When was that $60,600 spent in connection with the St. Leonard Fisheries, Limited?

I have not got the
date, but it was before my time. Even the North Sydney contract, the latest one in Nova Scotia, was entered into before I took charge of the department.

I should like to ask what
representations have been made to the minister in recent months on behalf of the fruit growers in the Maritime provinces, particularly in the Annapolis valley, for cold storage facilities. The minister will recall that the former member for Hants used to bring this matter to his attention annually, without very much success. I wonder if the department has looked into that, and whether it has made any provision for assistance?

I think my hon.
friend has not got just the slant on this matter which the former member for Hants had. He was not in favour of a regular cold storage plant; in fact, I recollect discussing the matter with him, and he was opposed to it. The weather is pretty cool in the fall in the Maritime provinces, and there has never been any strong request for pre-cooling facilities for their fruit. We did do a little bit in the way of ice storage, fixing up an old warehouse in the Annapolis valley in the fall of 1922, but the nights are so cold down there that the fruit will chill off in the barrels very nicely before going into storage. That is what these pre-cooling plants are required for, aud
Supply-Agriculture

we have had no demand from the Annapolis valley for a regular cold storage plant, probably on account of their climatic conditions. I do not just recall what the former member for Hants had in mind; perhaps the hon. member for York-Sunbury would refresh my mind. I know he was very much opposed to the project that we brought up at the first session with regard to co-operative cold storage. He had no use for that at all.

When this matter was before the House last year, the minister said that during the parliamentary recess he would reconsider the whole question of cold storage facilities. Agriculture is our great basic industry, and there is concurrent jurisdiction over it by the Dominion and the provinces. The provinces take the view that cold storage warehouses is a matter, under the British North America Act, for the federal government. The function of cold storage warehouses to-day is entirely different from what it was twenty-five years ago. Just the day before yesterday the first sod was turned of a new terminal warehouse in Toronto that is to cost $8,000,000. For twenty-five years we have looked to the federal government to do something in this matter, 'but nothing has been done, and the result is that the farmers have no place in which to store their butter and eggs and cheese and other products, and at the present time a large portion of these products goes to Montreal to be kept in cold storage in private warehouses. I think the minister has no conception of what this warehouse problem means to the producer and the consumer. The retailer to-day has to buy in advance of the market and has to keep in storage butter, eggs, cheese, apples and many other products, and he has to pay bank interest of course on his investment because of the lack of cold storage facilities. The farmer has to supply the credit, whereas if the government provided up-to-date warehouses at central points it would lessen the cost of production and also very largely reduce the cost to the consumer. One cannot fail to be impressed by the large number of officials attached to the Department of Agriculture, the heavy overhead and red tape of officialdom, and the consequent large expenditure in the way of salaries and other items which is involved. At a previous session we were promised some information about what other countries are doing in the way of providing modem terminal warehouses and other methods of assisting the farmers to market their products and to help in removing some of the peak load from the consumer. Go into

a grocery store to-day and you cannot get an apple for less than five cents, and the cost of such commodities as butter, cheese and eggs is in proportion. These prices are absolutely prohibitive to the working classes. A luncheon was held in Toronto the other day after the turning of the sod of the new terminal warehouse, a function which was attended by farmers from different points extending from Windsor east to Belleville, with the object of trying to see what could be done through the medium of private ownership to meet the problems pressing upon agriculturists. But problems of this kind should be worked out by the federal authorities. We have a Department of Agriculture here which is costing this country hundreds of thousands of dollars, and is staffed with officials from top to bottom. The department sends out every day loads of literature which is not read because it is too complicated. We want the federal government to take up this question, and carry out the promise made that some relief will be forthcoming to the agriculturists, the retailers, and the consumers. We ought in Canada to follow the plan with respect to terminal warehouses which has been adopted in every large city in the United States. Why is it necessary to bring in American capital to the extent of $8,000,000 to establish a terminal warehouse in Toronto to give relief to farmers in some 22 counties when the Dominion government has large resources and almost unlimited methods of taxation upon which it can draw in order to help the agricultural industry? Modem terminal warehouses are a modem economic necessity, both in the interest of producers and consumers and to lessen transportation costs and overhead. In the case of the former they would help to lessen the cost of production and of marketing, and there would be little or no waste. The retailer could buy to the best advantage when he needed supplies and those supplies would be in first-class condition. The consumer would benefit by being able to purchase commodities at a greatly reduced price. The problem has existed in an acute form since 1897 but notwithstanding the need for action no progress has been made. The federal and provincial governments have made a football of the question and whenever the provinces were urged to take action they have referred the applicants to the federal Minister of Agriculture. In central Ontario to-day the farmer is getting the worst of it. Many market, gardeners are abandoning their occupation, and the dairy industry is in a very precarious state. The railways do not provide proper accommodation; there is noth-

Supply-Agriculture
ing in the shape of proper storage facilities, there is not even a terminal elevator for grain in central Ontario, let alone a modem warehouse. There are practically no warehouses, except a few small ones that are operated on a very minor scale. The state of New York has dozens of these terminal warehouses. Every large city has them and the aid given by the federal authority is supplemented by grants from the state legislatures. We are making treaties all the time with outside countries, but we are doing little or nothing to help the farmers and the producers and also the consumers who are suffering so much from existing conditions. I think where private interests do this modern work a subsidy should be given to facilitate the construction of these terminal warehouses. They are not a luxury; they are a necessity. These warehouses should be either under the jurisdiction of the federal government, or else the federal authorities should grant money for the purpose to the provinces and let them work out a scheme. The Dominion government would get some revenue indirectly, and there would be an immense advantage to the farmer, the dairyman, the retailer and the consumer.

Allusion has been made
to the action taken by the member for Hants last year on the question of cold storage. I would remind the minister that the counties of Hants and Kings are now united. While it is true that the former member for Hants may not have voted for cold storage I suspect very strongly that one of the reasons why he is not sitting in this House to-day is because he did not understand the situation as clearly as was necessary and did not support cold storage for the Annapolis and Kings valley as strongly as he might have done. With reference to conditions in the two counties, we have been running to specialization in the matter of fruit for the last few years, but unfortunately we had three bad years in the fruit industry. May I say to the minister and to hon. members that the conditions in that regal'd were never worse in those two counties than they are to-day; and one special reason why I am here as a representative of these counties is because the federal government for the last four or five years, in fact for many years back, have not heeded the demands that have been made in the past and are still being pressed. I understand that several delegations composed of very substantial Liberals, from the two counties, have waited upon the government and impressed upon them the necessity of doing something 14011-141
to help the fruit industry of the Annapolis and Cornwallis valleys and of granting aid in other directions. The government instead of paying heed to these representations have appointed a commission to examine into conditions in the Maritime provinces. I venture to suggest that that commission was in no sense necessary. The members in this House supporting the government and members supporting the opposition are a unit on certain fundamental things which must be done in the Maritime provinces. A commission will not accomplish what is required. You cannot get these things done by appointing a royal commission and spending $25,000 or $50,000- probably this commission will cost $100,000 before iit is concluded.
Now with regard to the things which are required to be done, it is generally understood that we will have to get away from specialization in fruit growing in that section of the country if we are to make progress in creating greater wealth. The government will have to provide similiar facilities to those established elsewhere in Canada to assist the people to get back into the business of producing eggs, butter and cheese, meat, and so on; creameries will have to be established, and all those things are dependent upon cold storage facilities. We have before us to-day a propostion for a large cold storage warehouse for the city of Halifax. I understand it is to be undertaken by the Norcross Company, but the question who is to build it is of no particular interest, except in this way, that when representatives come from this section of the country and ask for assistance for cold storage institutions they ought to receive substantial consideration and support. I for one cannot vote millions of dollars to be spent in other sections of Canada, without drawing the attention of the minister and the government to the very important matter of voting at least some of this money to the re-creation of trade in the Maritime provinces to the end that there shall be an upbuilding of trade down there, in order to make two blades of grass, or two dollars, if you like, grow where one or none is growing or being earned at the present time.
On some of the items I will refer to particular industries, by which we will be able to produce millions of dollars worth of wealth in those counties if the government will give the matter some further attention. I am glad the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) is giving some attention to certain matters in that district, and I do not propose to find fault with him as to that. * But I desire very forcibly to direct his attention to the fact that

Supply-Agriculture

we must have new avenues for the production of wealth in those two counties of Hants-Kings and in that section of Nova Scotia in order to satisfy our people. If the Minister of Agriculture or even the Prime Minister were on the proposed Maritime commission, they would find conditions obtaining there pretty much as we have stated them during this session.
I hope it is not assumed that this item of $30,000 will be sufficient to take care of the situation in Halifax. I understand some further provision is to be made in the supplementary estimates. Even if the amount were $40,000 it would not take care of the situation or do much to revive the interest of the province in these matters. Of course this is only one of the things which can be done; other matters, such as freight rates, will come up in due course. I hope the minister will give instructions that when delegations of his own party from Nova Scotia come to him, they sLall be treated better than we would be if we approached him. It is not a question of being magnanimous to any particular part of the country; but it is a matter of seeing that the money v'hich is spent will be productive of new wealth and of prosperity which does not now exist.

I wish my hon. friend would refresh my memory with regard to requests for the establishment of a cold storage plant in Nova Scotia, outside of the city of Halifax. The understanding was that Halifax could not be taken care of in this vote. I have no recollection of refusing any cold storage plant in Nova Scotia. We have been doing something in reference to the establishment of cold storage in the Annapolis valley, but outside of that we have not established any plants. We are not promoting these things ourselves, but we are putting 30 per cent into the enterprise to help those who help themselves. I believe the hon. member (Mr. Spence) is pretty well posted on this question, and I do not think he will take the ground that we need a lot more cold storage plants.
I do not think I heard all that the hon. member for Toronto Northwest (Mr. Church) said a few minuts ago, but he spoke gaily in terms of eight or more millions. I am afraid I would shock the House if I brought down a measure which would pretend to take care of an enterprise of that nature. Neither this vote nor any previous vote was intended to take care entirely of port situations. The enterprise at Montreal is one of the finest on the continent, and I would like to give my predecessors full credit for that. It is very
IMr. Forke.]
much required. I think it has been capable of taking care of the cold storage business that has been offering at that port ever since. But the proposition of cold storage immediately after the war was a very doubtful one, for the simple reason that the people were not patronizing these warehouses. They were not storing their produce; they were retrenching and using the facilities around home, buying a small plant and putting it in their kitchen or basement, and storing their dairy produce there instead of keeping it in a public cold storage where they had to pay for it; consequently there was not a demand for storage. There is not one single new contract for this year. Yet we have not been refusing them, outside of Halifax, and it was not really a refusal. I drew the attention of the senior member for Halifax (Mr. Black) to the fact that this vote was never intended to take care of cold storage at the port of Halifax, because that would run into a large sum. If I understand the hon. member for Toronto Northwest rightly, there is the prospect of a great enterprise, running into millions, being established in Toronto. That is not a pure cold storage proposition. A cold storage warehouse, like an elevator, seldom can pay its way when it relies merely on the charges for storing produce. Whoever owns such a warehouse must be a large produce dealer, must trade in this produce and must obtain profits largely in that way. These things seldom take care of the cost of operation and of storing the produce when the crops come in.
I should like to assure hon. members opposite, and all hon. members in the House generally, that this vote will take care of all the projects now under way, and the first one is at North Sydney, in the province of the hon. member for Hants. It is a general cold storage for all kinds of commodities. Later on in the session it will be taken up and considered.
I may say, from a cursory examination of the Maritimes, which I had the honour of making two years ago, one of the first impressions I got was that the plan for the development of the fishing industry at Halifax was lamentably short in cold storage facilities. Furthermore, if the trade with the West Indies develops as we expect it will under the new treaty, we will require more accommodation for perishable goods arriving at Halifax dock from the West Indies, in order that they may be taken care of, until distribution is made by the various railways and through other avenues. Therefore, I feel

Supply-A griculture
somewhat sympathetic with the Halifax project. But this was never intended to include port cold storage. It is too large a proposition to be included ,'n this vote.

After trying to hear what is going on in the House, I have been wondering if there is any good reason why the business of this Dominion should be carried on in such a manner that one part of the House is not able to follow the discussion intelligently.

I was asking the minister a few minutes ago where the cold storage plants in Nova Scotia were situated. He stated one was St. Leonard Fisheries Limited at Port Hawkesbury and that $60,000 was appropriated for that. That is purely a fish cold storage plant. I do not object to the vote, but why does it come under the Department of Agriculture?
Fish is one of the natural resources of the country. These things interlock sometimes. Does my hon. friend want to put in a claim to have it refunded?

No, but why should fish
come under the Department of Agriculture?

That was before
my time and I had nothing to do with it. I have not the year in which it was initiated, but I happen to know that fisheries are included in this vote because I know in other parts of Canada agriculture was interpreted to apply to fisheries as well as to agriculture, not of course to apply exclusively to fish because it is not advisable to have perishable commodities like dairy produce in the same warehouse as fish. We try to avoid that but the old interpretation in regard to agriculture included fish. Those who come from the Pacific coast and are familiar with conditions at Prince Rupert will know that a considerable sum was given in years past to a fish cold storage plant at that point. My deputy informs me that the plant was intended to be for everything, but as a matter of fact it has developed largely in connection with the cold storage of fish.
Are we to understand that all cold storage plants in Canada ai;e under the Department of Agriculture?
No.

Then why is this plant at Port Hawkesbury, where no agricultural products are stored, under the Department of Agriculture?
14011-141J

That is away back in days gone by. It is hard to learn how we got into it. I have pointed out that port plants, such as the one at Montreal, are not under our department but under harbour boards. That is the exception.

Are all these plants in
Nova Scotia used chiefly for fish cold storage or are some of them used for agricultural purposes?

The one at North Sydney, for instance, is used for agricultural purposes and fish as well, but we have to take special precautions in connection with insulating the plant and dividing it off into rooms to ensure that no offensive odours from the fish contaminate other commodities that are stored there.

Of course the minister does not contend that the cold storage plant at North Sydney is in aid of agriculture. If he does, he had better revise his ideas regarding that part of the country. Is the cold storage proposition at Montreal assisted out of this vote?
No.
Is that done through the harbour commission?
Yes, entirely.

Does the government or any department of the government obtain a report from the harbour commission as to the business done in its cold storage branch? Is the minister able to tell us whether that is a money making proposition or not?

I would imagine
there would be a report each year to the Department of Marine and Fisheries under which I understand it comes. Our officers are almost constantly employed in the plant grading butter and cheese; we are fairly familiar with the kind of service that is given and it is satisfactory.

Are butter and
cheese products of the sea, as the cold storage plant at Montreal appears to be under the Department of Marine and Fisheries?

conferences we have had regarding butter and cheese boxes it has been decided that the word "Canada" shall be conspiciously displayed on all containers.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.
After Recess
The committee resumed at eight o'clock.

Mr. Chairman, I should
like to ask the minister what grades of apples are most popular in the British market.

Replying to a
question put by the hon. member for Victoria (Mr. Tolmie) before dinner, I am informed that the total export of apples has remained almost stationary at about two million barrels per annum. There was a five per cent decrease this year, due largely, I think, to the very early frost of last October that rendered a lot of Ontario apples useless for export. As to the most papular grade in the British market, as a rule the people in the Old Country prefer the high grade apples of British Columbia. But I do not want to be misunderstood with regard to Nova Scotia apples; if they were as well taken care of in the process of packing as those of British Columbia and received shipping point inspection, I think they would! regain their past reputation. Unfortunately, there is a little carelessness in
packing practised by some exporters with the hope of "getting away" with it. In fact, whether it be wheat, apples, or any other commodity, there is a disposition to try to get past the official grader with something that is not quite up to grade. Therefore, all grading has to be done very carefully. To the extent that exporters are careless in maintaining their grades they tend to destroy whatever reputation their commodity may have on the British market.

Does the minister include
boxes among the barrels he quoted?
Yes, the total export is reduced to terms of barrels.

I understand the minister
to say that No. 1 apples are in greater demand than No. 2.
That is my information.

Do the higher priced No.
1 apples meet the demand of the poorer class of consumers?

I would not think
so, for very frequently they buy the cheaper artide. That is the reason why sometimes they prefer a mixed lot, for it enables the parents of large families to distribute a small apple to each child.

I understand that in Scotch families, which are usually large, they prefer the No. 2 grade because the smaller size gives them a greater number of apples, which enables the parents to distribute an apple apiece among their children. What measures are being taken by the government to advertise our agricultural products in reat Britain? With the high tariff in the United States, the Old Country affords us our principal opportunity to sell our surplus, and I think it is very necessary to bring to the attention of the British people the fine quality of our bacon, ham, fruit, dairy products, and so forth, the better to enable us to compete with our sister dominions and with Denmark, Holland and other countries. What is being done in this "direction, or is it left entirely to private enterprise?

We have various
ways of advertising our products. The Canadian Fruit Show that has been -held in England annually for the last four years has helped to advertise our apples, and we advertise in two or three British publications. But I think we got the best advertising results with the least expenditure of money at a
Supply-Agriculture

dinner in the Hotel Cecil, held under the auspices of our agricultural representative in Great Britain. All the courses consisted of Canadian-grown products, and as the two or three hundred guests were leaving-
What about the wine?

If I remember
rightly it was Ontario wine, but I do not know whether that would satisfy the British taste. Anyway, they smoked our Canadian cigars. As the guests were leaving, each was given a hamper with samples of all those Canadian-*grown products. These hampers they took home to their wives, sisters or sweethearts, as the case might be, and the advertising effect was excellent. As a matter of fact we got a number of unsolicited compliments on its effectiveness. During the Wembley exhibition we had our products placed on the menu cards of the restaurants within the exhibition grounds, and of those throughout London operated by the Lyons Company.

Wlhat brands of liquid
refreshments did they dispense?
It has been suggested that the native wines of Ontario were given the place of honour.

I am glad to hear that the minister has adopted this method of bringing our Canadian products before the people of Great Britain. He has said something about sweethearts. I do not know of any better way of winning sweethearts in England than by tempting them with a few Okanagan apples. What periodicals or newspapers does the department advertise in, and to what extent?

We have some
small advertisements in Canada, The Canadian Export Pioneer, and we also advertise in the Canadian Gazette. Of course, advertising in newspapers cannot compare with the advertising that our producers get by delivering the goods, and in any case it is rather an expensive business carrying advertisements on any large scale in magazines and* periodicals. Our cheese was exceedingly well advertised at Wembley through the menu cards of the restaurants, and especially through the Lyons Company, for almost a year. Its reputation has been so enhanced as to be almost at its pre-war eminence.

Now that the Wembley
exhibition is over, does the department intend to exhibit at the Royal Show in Great Britain?
That, I understand, is a perambulating affair.
The show is held in a different place each year.

W'hile it is important that we should be advertised at these fairs, we must at the same time be governed by the amount of money at our disposal. We exhibit at the London dairy show, which embraces not only dairy products proper but bacon, eggs and so on.

I am glad that the minister intends to continue advertising in this way. There is this point to be emphasized however: if we are going to exhibit our products in Great Britain we should see to it that they are equal to or, preferably, better than those shown by the other dominions. On one occasion when I was in the Old Country I noticed at the Royal Show that while Canada's exhibit did not convey anything like an adequate idea of what this country could produce, South Africa had a wonderful display which attracted considerable attention and which was crowded all the time. Such an exhibit as ours in competition with the magnificent exhibits of South Africa and Australia can only do us harm rather than good. If we are going to exhibit at all we should do it fairly well.
That is right. Our Toronto packers, I am pleased to say, for the last two years in succession have taken the highest award in bacon.

I
understand that year before last representations were made to the minister regarding the necessity for standardizing turnips. This is an important product in my section. I believe that a number of inspections were made with the idea of arriving at some standard rules to govern the grading of this vegetable. Has anything been done in that direction?
I have no recollection of the matter.

Perhaps the minister will recall it if I read a brief paragraph from his report ending March 31, 1925:
A service along the above lines, but for educational purposes, by our regular staff, was provided as an experiment on request of the Ontario Turnip Shippers' Association to cover some forty-two loading stations in western Ontario. Five inspectors were detailed for this work making inspections of some 460 cars. The inspections were made on the basis of tentative grades, approved by the Ontario Turnip Growers' Association and the department, and may provide a basis for re-

Supply-Agriculture
commending legislation in the near future as the industry feels the necessity for standardization in order to compete successfully with graded stock, particularly on the United States market.

I remember now.
It was not an official grading, the arrangement having been made between the vegetable growers themselves. There is no official grading of turnips, but it frequently happens that a practice initiated by producers themselves in a small way like this leads up to official action. The same process is taking place in connection with the exporting of honey. No recognized grades of honey have been established, but the beekeepers have decided upon certain grades of their own and the system is assuming such importance as will probably warrant our taking cognizance of it and providing for a grade under which this com-, modity may be placed on a foreign market.
Nothing has been done yet?
No.

What progress has been
made by the British Economic Committee in the matter of fruit?

A voluminous report has been submitted on the subject. Mr. Forsythe Smith, with the assistance of one or two others, has prepared some 200 odd pages *which he expects to have ready for the public at any moment. We have some confidential advance information with reference to the subject but I think that possibly it would be better not to give it at present.
Does the minister understand that the British government has made no progress in relation to the grant which was supposed to be given towards marketing?

That is not for fruit
only.

It is intended to
include dairy products. We shall have a representative over there assisting Mr. Forsythe Smith and working in conjunction with the others as Mr. McOuat did in connection with the meat report.

I have read a good deal
of the debates that have taken place on this item in the past three or four years and I have come to the conclusion that the minister has lost track of the main thing in giving the fruit growers adequate protection. Representing a constituency in the Toronto district which is near the Niagara peninsula,
I have been amazed to see how little has been done to safeguard the fruit industry and to stimulate the production of our own fruits and vegetables. I do not know of any country in the world where Providence has done so much and man so little to develop this industry. Our lack of a national policy herein is deplorable. What does the minister propose to do to protect this industry? Nothing. A return that was brought down last year, and which will be found in Hansard, shows the tremendous amount of fruit and vegetables that is imported into this country and the extent to which there is dumping of American fruits. The amount is perfectly staggering; it has ruined our own fruit farms. This industry up to a few years ago used to provide work for a good many people in this country; it used to be one of our basic agricultural industries in Ontario, but to-day it is withering away. In two or three seasons throughout the year we have large importations of tropical fruits, which works to the disadvantage of our own producers. In all the large departmental stores in the large cities and towns of this country you will find piles of American fruit which has been imported into Canada at a- great loss to our own fruit growers. Many of the fruit farms in the district from which I come have been sold. The industry has decayed, and you cannot put it on its feet unless the government provides proper cold storage facilities and adequate safeguarding legislation. Saskatchewan may have become the Washington of the north, the centre of gravity as it were, temporarily for Canada; but what does the minister propose to do during the next twelve months to protect this industry, which is now dying away so far as the province of Ontario is concerned? It is not like it was twenty-five years ago, simply because of the absence of a definite national policy on the part of this government; there is no vision. Years ago boats plied on all the Great Lakes carrying for a very few cents per one hundred pounds fruit that had been grown in the Toronto-Niagara district, but to-day there is a steamship monopoly on the Great Lakes, and it is going to interfere seriously with the fruit growing industry in the Niagara district. A combine and monopoly exists.
Now, what about the consumer? It is proposed to spend a few hundred thousand dollars again this year the same as last, to pay the salaries of a large number of officials,
Supply-Agriculture

but what does the government propose to do to protect this industry in all the provinces? Take the apple industry, for instance. Where is that industry to-day? Years ago you could go into a store and buy apples by the peck or by the bag for a very low price, but to-day they are charging the working classes in my district five and seven cents for just one apple, while we appoint paper commissions on the tariff to kill time; the government is spending in this vote tqp much money on overhead. Look what Ohio, New York, Indiana and Michigan are doing to protect the fruit industry there. Ohio is a state with 10,000,000 of people, about the size of Canada, and the state legislature has put this industry on its feet, with the result that all through the summer on lakes Erie and Ontario steamers are plying across the lake loaded with American fruit and vegetables from that state, and landed at Port Stanley and other points on lake Ontario. What sort of national policy is this government going to evolve to protect the fruit industry in this country, to prevent the invasion of Canada by American products, to prevent this country from becoming the happy hunting ground for all the Yankee fruit growers on the North American continent while the policy of drift continues? It is the Americans who are getting the cream of the Canadian business in fruit and vegetables. What does the government propose to do in the next twelve months to safeguard the fruit industry in Canada from coast to coast, and this industry in particular?

I think I would be usurping the functions of the new advisory tariff board if 1 were to take this matter up. I would, therefore, suggest that we leave it to the board which has been constituted, and which will possibly be functioning within a few days. It is not within my province to announce a national policy with respect to the tariff. We will be advised on the tariff by the board that has recently been appointed, and I cannot predict what they will or will not do, but doubtless all these arguments that are being advanced by my hon. friend will be taken into consideration by the board.

As a result of the lack of a policy on the part of the government on this question, the mass production of the United States in fruit and vegetables is being brought across the border in motor trucks from Buffalo and the Yankees are getting the cream of the business and using Canada as 
a dumping yard. That is what happens under the absence of any sensible policy of this government, and it is no wonder the Americans are finding Canada a happy hunting ground and are grabbing everything so far as this industry is concerned while all we do is talk about useless tariff commissions.

The minister a moment ago hid behind what he called the new advisory tariff board. I wish to make just one remark, Mr. Chairman, and it is that the order in council appointing this new board never said one word about "advisory". No such word is used in it at all, but we have heard tke word used by the Prime Minister and now by the Minister of Agriculture. This board is not advisory at all; it is simply tader the dictation of the Minister of Finance.

I think my hon.
friend is wrong. He will find that the regulations indicate the advisory character of the board.

It would be appropriate
if the minister at this time would tell us what he and his department have been doing to facilitate the marketing of the products of the farms of Canada. There is no question that that is the great problem before this country. There has been plenty of evidence this afternoon to show that the spread between the producer and the consumer is enormous, and it is the duty of this department and of the government to reduce that spread so that the producer will get a larger share of the ultimate price paid for his product. If there is one thing which this government ought to do but which they are not doing, it is to help the farmers of this country market their products in such a way that they will get greater remuneration for their products. I would ask the minister what his department is doing along that line.

We have been on
that very question all day. Was my hon. friend not in? Anything that will help to improve the quality of an article will help to market it. It is clearly understood that anything that is well bought is half sold; anj'thing of high quality will help to sell itself. If we see that the product is properly graded and put on the market in the" proper way. especially the article for export, which determines our reputation abroad, that naturally assists in the marketing of the product. I do not know what my hon. friend had particularly in mind. Was it transportation?

Supply-A gricul ture

I have in mind the fact that the ultimate price paid for the article should go into the pockets of the producer, not into the pockets of the middleman, as it is going to-day, and I think the minister and his department are asleep in that respect. The profits are going to the middleman, not to the man who is producing the article. The minister has been asleep for the last five years, and has not yet wakened up to that fact.
Oh, oh.

The minister says "Oh,
oh." I leave it to the producer of agricultural products to say whether or not I am right. Why, we have had this very day proof of the enormous prices that have been paid for commodities-apples, for instance-by the consumer. Those profits are not going into the pockets of the producer. Yet this government is unconscious of the duty it owes to the producers of this country, and of the necessity of enunciating a policy which will ensure to the producer a greater share of the profits which are now being enjoyed by the middleman.
I presume that what my hon. friend has now in mind is the cooperative marketing of farm products?

Yes, it is one of the
things.

Well, if my hon.
friend knew the history of that movement he would know that no province has done so much in that respect as Saskatchewan. That is essentially a provincial matter.

I am talking about the
responsibility of this government, not about the responsibilities of the provinces.

We are talking about the government that has to do with cooperative marketing, and that is essentially a provincial matter. That may not have been drawn to my hon. friend's attention. During the time I had the honour to act in a provincial capacity the foundation was laid for those co-operative activities that are today the largest of their kind, not only on this continent but in the entire world. My hon. friends think I should follow the provincial activities into the federal field. I am afraid that in some respects we are doing that now We have been trying to draw the line of demarcation between provincial and federal activities, leaving the production and the educational branches, if you can call them so, to the provinces, while the federal authority
takes care of the grading, the marketing, the care of the health of animals and like matters. It is not an easy thing to draw the line, because these various activities overlap in spite of us. We have been working harmoniously,
I think, with every province in that respect. In no part of Canada do we do as much work that is really provincial as we do in the maritime provinces. In Ontario I have been in communication with the Hon. John Martin, by correspondence and otherwise, about some work we have been doing in connection with the testing of cattle for butter fat, there being a general disposition as 'between the federal department and the provincial government to keep the line of demarcation between the respective jurisdictions. It is admitted that as the work of co-operative marketing develops we shall derive very beneficial results. But what would my hon. friends have the federal government do in the matter? Open wholesale or retail houses, and out out all the middlemen? How would my hon. friend himself proceed?

I would not hide behind the provinces and get rid of responsibility in that way. I would take hold of my department and run it so that the consumer would get the benefit of the policies which I inaugurated.
Oh, well, that is a little bit of grandstand play.

The minister is an
adept at that himself; if there is anyone in the House who surpasses all others in grandstand play it is the minister.

When I was in
the Saskatchewan legislature, for the first time in the history of any province estimates were introduced for the purchase of cream, provision being made that the treasury should be recouped.
That is not fruit.

I am talking about co-operative marketing. I am not averse to learning from any source. I am prepared to accept information from my hon. friend or anyone else; that is the way I learn. But I would remind my hon. friend that he cannot tack such a thing on to the federal department because we would be exceeding our prerogative if we undertook work of that nature.

Did you do that
when you established the wheat board?
Supply-Agriculture

We have the market prices broadcast to the farmers by radio. We have a regular marketing branch to give the farmers information as to the condition of the markets so that they will know when they go to those markets that they are getting full value for their products.

They could get it
through the daily newspapers.

Let me be quite
candid: I am not at all averse to getting all the information I can as to how to improve my department. I would be delighted to get information from any source whereby we would be able to narrow that spread my hon. friend speaks of. I can recall that before my hon. friend entered this House I brought down a bill with respect to the establishment of cold storage plants, expressly for the purpose of developing the spirit of co-operation and encouraging co-operative salesmanship among our farmers. What kind of reception did that bill get from the associates of my hon. friend? What kind of reception did it get in the Senate after hon. members had hammered the life out of it here? The bill got through here but it did not get through the Senate. It was so badly mutilated there that it was no good and I had to abandon it. So my hon. friend should know a little bit about the history of these matters before he gets up and proclaims from the housetop how the federal department should exercise provincial prerogatives without ai the same time invading the provincial field. If my hon. friend has any suggestions to make as to work that will come within my jurisdiction I shall be delighted to welcome them, because there is no doubt there is a spread. But my hon. friend wants to narrow the spread by increasing the duties. He says that by making products dearer you are going to narrow the spread.

No, I want to narrow
the spread by cutting out the profits of the middleman and giving them to the consumer. The minister and the government during the last five years have been asleep to the necessity of doing that, and they are still in a comatose condition.

I suggest to my
hon. friend- that he should apply to the provincial government; and there is a good Department of Agriculture in this province.
Have they any control over the export of food products?

Oh, well, we will
attend to the exports.

In support of the position taken by the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario, let me read just a few lines from the report of the Department of Agriculture which, I think, will convince even the minister that the hon. member was justified in taking the position he did. On page 40 of that report I find the following:
Additional illustrations could be given indicative of the weak points in our live stock industry as having reference to its development as a national business. The fact that Great Britain imports $168,000,000 of bacon and pork products per annum, Canada at present supplying only 15 per cent of this amount, confirms the above statement both with reference to our problem and to our national opportunity.
Surely that is a national question which the minister should take up. When we are only supplying IS per cent to a market which consumes $168,000,000 a year there is surely ground for the minister's bringing about improvements in that regard.

Is the situation
better or worse than it was three or four years ago? My hon. friend has heard it stated that the quality of our product is improving, that the spread between Canadian and Danish bacon is narrowing every year. Three years ago there was a spread of from twenty to twenty-five cents between Canadian and Danish bacon. To-day both products quite frequently are on a parity, with probably a difference of five shillings per hundred, or from that to two or three shillings at other times, showing an improvement not only in quantity but in quality. Now that is the national part that comes under the prerogative of the federal department, as I understand it. But notwithstanding that fact we are, in a measure, working with the provincial government. That responsibility is always imposed upon us because associated with grading there must always be efforts to improve quality. It is just a question where we should stop the one and commence the other. But my hon. friend thinks that because Great Britain does not buy all this bacon from Canada somebody is derelict in his duty.

I am not asking that they buy all of it from Canada, but when Great Britain is buying $168,000,000 of the very products the minister has been talking about, and we are only able to furnish 15 per cent of them, I think it is about time the minister woke up and took a more active interest in the department.

Supply-Agriculture

Thank you. I will just tell the result of the waking up. For a great many years during the administration of the friends of my hon. friend there was an embargo on Canadian cattle going to the Old Country.

That is an old story.
Who helped to get the embargo off?

There was a total
embargo; you could not ship store cattle into Great Britain. What did you do? Was it not an international enterprise we went into?
I am always willing to give credit to hon. gentlemen opposite for anything they did. The hon. member for South Winnipeg deserves credit for the work he did in connection with it, but the fact remains that this is the government which succeeded in having the embargo removed.
Oh, no.

Oh, yes. You will
have to get up earlier in the morning before you can spring anything like that on me. It was suggested this afternoon that I should educate the Maritime people with regard to certain matters. Well, I am willing to sit at the feet of my hon. friend across the way, but they must not be threshing old, straw and making allegations in which there is absolutely nothing with respect to dereliction of duty on the part of this government in regard to our live stock market. We have succeeded in. inducing the British government to open a market which has been closed for thirty years. Is that a fact or not?
No, no.

It does not matter
what my hon. friends may think of the method or of the enterprise, but last year when we endeavoured to meet that situation and prepare Canada for the inevitable time when we had to compete with the Argentine in live cattle, what did my hon. friends do? They opposed it to a man.

What did the committee
of the minister's own government do but throw out the contract?

What did my hon.
friend do?

My hon. friend does not
like the truth.
The committee was a committee of parliament and got its cue from my hon. friends.
It was a committee of this government.
lit does not matter whether it was the best method or not; it was the best in sight. My hon. friend was not in the House, but his party is on record, both then and previously, and did nothing.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I call attention to the fact that we are discussing item 42.

With reference to the
statement of the hon. Minister of Agriculture in regard to the embargo and to certain inaccuracies in connection therewith, I should like the privilege of saying four or five words in that connection. Looking back through the history of the cattle embargo, we know that it was in existence for thirty years. On that point the minister is quite correct. 1 should like to point out that the first break or the first change in the situation in connection with the cattle embargo was a promise to the Right Hon. Sir Robert Borden, who was then Prime Minister of the country. That right hon. gentleman and the hon. member for South Winnipeg held a conference with the representatives of the British government including the then Minister of Agriculture, and it was on that occasion that the British government promised to lift the embargo at the conclusion of the war. After that an embargo commission was created by the British government and the case for Canada was presented to that commission by the Conservative government of the day. ,At that particular time a promise was secured from the then Minister of Agriculture to the effect that the government of Great Britain would be guided by the finding of that embargo commission. That, commission found in our favour. The legislation was then introduced into the British House of Commons, and all the present government had to do with it, so far as I am aware, was in helping to make some regulations, or to come to some agreement with regard to regulations, as to how those Canadian cattle could enter Great Britain.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Will the committee
proceed to the item under discussion?

Did the minister make
the statement that the present government was responsible for the removal of the embargo?

I think the hon.
member for Marquette claimed that distinction. He lifted the embargo.
Supply-Agricxdture

I never made that statement. If the minister says I did he is incorrect. It is not the fact. I think I had something to do with it. I think the minister had some correspondence with me in regard to it. I do not think the minister has the right to make the claim which he has made in regard to the removal of the embargo, and I will tell him that he only left the job half finished. If Canada had obtained justice she would have the Canadian cow in on the open market, instead of having her where she is. There would be no trouble at all if there was some effort to induce the British authorities now to consent to the admission of the Canadian cow on the British market. True, we got the males in, but that was not the result of the efforts of the present government. An hon. member sitting over here, who is not making any statement at all, is the gentleman responsible for having the embargo removed.
I referred to the hon. member.

They exacted promises and that is what accomplished the result. Public men in Great Britain stated on the platform that while they did not want to admit our cattle, still they were going to keep the promise they made to Sir Robert Borden and the hon. gentleman from South Winnipeg. I do not think it is fair for hon. members on the other side of the House to claim credit for the removal of the embargo.

The item is a fairly large one, $200,000, and the question asked by the hon. member for Mus-koka-Ontario was a very pertinent one. He asked what the government was doing in regard to the marketing of fruit, particularly apples. Apples are grown in many places in Ontario. The trees grow quite naturally and bear a certain kind of fruit, which indicates that the province is by nature adapted to the growing of apples, and I believe there are millions of bushels annually going to waste in Ontario; orchards are being neglected and the people are not taking full advantage of their opportunities. The minister endeavoured to say that this was a matter for the provinces to deal with, not the federal government. He indicated the strides which had been made by the province of Saskatchewan in this respect. Perhaps he would inform the House what Saskatchewan has really done in regard to the marketing of apples.
We do not grow any apples of any account.

I quite understand that, and I did not think the minister's reference to Saskatchewan, in view of the question asked by the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario, was an answer at all. There are great difficulties in the way of marketing fruit, particularly apples, and I notice by the returns of the trade of Canada that our apples are exported to about twenty-five different countries. The minister states that their responsibility ends when they see that the fruit is put on the market in the proper way. But apparently no effort is being made by the department to assist in the marketing of fruit. There must be something done along that line in the matter of cooperative marketing if we are going to reap the advantages which we should, and I think the federal department is the proper one to take steps in the_ matter. When the present government came into office there was an annual grant of about one million dollars a year under what was known as the Agricultural Instruction Act, which was being divided up amongst the seven provinces and which could be used with great benefit along this line. I should like to ask the minister if one of the first steps he took when he came into office was not to have an analysis made as to the value received for the money voted under the [DOT] Agricultural Instruction Act. A report was made to the minister by the party whom he appointed for this purpose favouring the continuance of the Agricultural Instruction Act and pointing out the advantages which were derived from the money voted for it. If the minister was consistent in what he stated when this matter was brought up in the House, namely, that this commissioner, as he termed him.-although he never was a commissioner-was appointed for that purpose, why did he not act on the recommendation which the commisioner made, which the minister has and in which the commissioner pointed out the advantages of continuing this aid to agriculture under the Agricultural Instruction Act? The minister in that way could co-operate with the provinces and do something along this line. Co-operative marketing is something that must be put into operation in this country and assisted if we are to obtain the advantages to which we are naturally entitled.
Cold storage facilities and all the means of transport are under the control of the federal government, and surely the minister does not mean to say that this matter rests entirely with the provinces. It is the duty of the federal government to assist the provinces and to get them to co-operate and to co-

Supply-Agriculture
ordinate in this matter. I do not 'believe there is anything of greater importance to those engaged in fruit growing in Canada than to enable them to co-operate so as to place their produce on the market with a good deal of unnecessary expense eliminated. It is a downright shame to see the hundreds of thousands of barrels of first class fruit that annually goes to waste in Ontario and something should be done to prevent it. The minister says that some of the provinces have already taken over the work which was done by the federal government in the past. That may be true as regards some provinces, but the federal government does not and never has assisted in any way the fruit growing industry in Ontario; it has left the matter entirely to the provincial government.

The cold storage
plant at Grimsby is a very useful institution.

I
am speaking about the experimental stations, because these are being contributed to by Ontario and other provinces. Nevertheless, nothing is being done in this province and the minister says: The matter must rest entirely with the province; we are not going to do anything in the matter of marketing fruit, so we shall vote just $200,000, appoint an army of inspectors to go around the country, and our responsibility will end there. Surely the minister does not mean to leave on the members of this House the impression that the responsibility of the government ends with the appointment Of an army of officials. By the way, the minister has put forth great efforts to see that a change is made in the complexion of the inspectors whom he found in office when he came in. I have in mind two seasonal inspectors in the county from which I come, both appointed about the same time and both thoroughly competent men, who received notices from the department asking them for their resignations shortly after the minister took office.
