I do not think we
could recommend a fertilizer unless we knew what it was required for, any more than a doctor could prescribe a medicine without knowing what was wrong with the patient.
Does the department not make recommendations in this pamphlet on fertilizers?

If the minister
would let the deputy stand up he would explain what my question refers to.
What does my hon. friend want? Is that not plain?
It is not an answer to my question at all.
What does my hon. friend want? Let me repeat, Mr. Chairman, there is no such thing as "best" fertilizer. It depends on the crop to be grown and the land you are dealing with.
I think the minister said that every domestic manufacturer had to take out a license. How many Canadian manufacturers have done so in the last year?
Approximately fifty. I have had correspondence with a good many myself, but I cannot recollect them all. Most of them were in the Maritime provinces, some in Ontario.

Surely the minister does not intend to convey the idea that our experimental farms are not in a position to recommend the kinds of fertilizers which should be used in certain districts and soils? I think that is the information the hon. member for Kingston City (Mr. Ross) desires.
I tried to make that plain. The best way I think to illustrate that is to ask: Could any medical man prescribe a flat dose for my hon. friend, no matter what was the matter with him?

He might for the hon.
minister.
That might be.

After a little rest, Mr. Chairman, may I point out to the minister that his department issues a bulletin on fertilizers which contains certain recommendations. Now, does he not know that that pamphlet is being issued? If one is not sent to him I will hand him my copy.

We are issuing those bulletins continually. Supposing we are dealing with the Maritime provinces, where they grow potatoes largely and use certain fertilizers, we would always have an eye single to what the fertilizer was to be used for; we would not issue the same instructions for that part of the country as we would to some other part where a different
crop was being grown and where an entirely different fertilizer would be required. Would my hon. friend from Kingston, as a medical man, issue the same kind of prescription for everybody?

If I were administering the department I would be willing to answer any questions. The bulletin does not say that the fertilizer is for Nova Scotia, Cape Breton, or Ontario; it gives the composition and recommends it. I was trying to get the minister out of a difficulty by m(y question, but it is impossible.

Every fertilizer contains three essential ingredients: nitrogen, potash and phosphoric acid. The proportions of these ingredients vary according to the particular crop you intend to grow and the deficiency of the soil in any of these chemical elements.

In some parts, particularly in the east, the farmers use what they call home-mixed fertilizers. They purchase the chemicals and do the mixing themselves. The results are very successful and they save considerable money in this way. Is any effort being made by the department to determine the purity of these chemicals? It is very important that the imported ingredients shall be exactly what they are represented to be.
Yes, the chief work of the branch is to see that the imported stuff is what it is supposed to be, and worth the money for manurial purposes. Their inspection discloses any spurious contents.

Mr. Chairman, on page 6 of the bulletin to which the hon. member for Kingston (Mr. Ross) has drawn attention I find that prices of Belgian basic slag of sixteen per cent analysis are quoted for the Maritime provinces and elsewhere. Will the minister tell us why the price of Nova Scotia slag is not quoted?
I remember we discussed the question two or three years ago. Basic slag is the by-product of the Sydney smelter?
Yes.
I understand that it is all exported; there is none placed on the home market.

Mr. Chairman, for the information of the minister I may tell him that it is not being exported. It is not on the home market, as he says, but for a very
Supply-Agriculture

different reason-because that plant has been forced to close down by the importation of Belgian and other slag, [DOT] which importation has been stimulated by lowering the duty. That industry in the Maritime provinces i3 entirely wiped out. I took some interest, naturally because it was a matter of great importance to our people, to find out whether or not the farmers were getting their fertilizer any cheaper by virtue of the fact that this industry was put out of business. I find that after they succeeded in closing down our industry the price of fertilizer in the Maritime provinces advanced three dollars a ton, and there is intimation of another two dollar raise, which seems to be the old story repeating itself, that directly the local manufacturer is put out of business the foreign monopolists put up the prices to whatever limit they see fit. I am forced to the conclusion that it is no use trying to impress upon this government that industry is of value in the Maritime provinces, or in any other part of Canada, because a moment ago I tried to get from the Prime Minister before he left the House an expression of opinion on a very important item that was promised by the Minister of Agriculture, but before he got around to it he was shut off by the Chairman, who called the item and it was passed. So I despair of getting any assistance at all from the minister so far as this item is concerned, and I merely rise to tell him that the government succeeded in putting the local industry out of business. *

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I must direct the hon. member's attention to the fact that I did not shut off discussion and I cal! upon him to withdraw his statement.

Mr. Chairman, I think I can throw some light on this subject, although not from personal knowledge. It was brought up last year or the year before, and a statement similar to that repeated now by my hon. friend opposite was then made, that owing to the reduction of the duty on fertilizers the plant at some particular place in Nova Scotia had been ruined. A few weeks later an hon. member on this side of the House, whose constituency was immediately adjoining that in which the plant is located, said he would give the real explanation of why the plant was closed down-in the first place he said, it had not closed down since the change in the duty, it had been closed down two years and a half before the reduction was made. In the second place he explained the reason for the closing down of the plant. This basic slag, which is a byproduct of steel, they had been selling to the
(Mr. Foster.]
farmers as an article which analysis and experience had proved to be good. In the course of time the particular works from which this by-product was mad'- changed their system of making steel from the open hearth to the Bessemer method, or vice versa -I do not know which. At any rate they changed the system with the result that the basic slag, while it would still give a chemical analysis, had lost its value as a fertilizer by reason of the fact that it was no longer soluble in water. And this notwithstanding they continued, either in ignorance or deliberately, to sell this non-fertilizing basic slag to the farmers of the neighbourhood until by bitter experience the farmers discovered the difference and ceased to buy it, the consequence being that the fertilizer plant went out of existence. That was the Charge which was made on the other side of the House and which was answered on this side, as will be seen by reference to Hansard. Just before I close let me reply to an hon. member opposite who made the statement that there were no fertilizer plants in Canada now. There are three in British Columbia at the present time, all doing an increasing business.

I rise in order to restate
what I said before. I had no desire, Mr. Chairman, to intimate that the shutting off of the discussion was deliberate on your part. I merely suggested that the Prime Minister was unable to speak, as had been suggested by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) in answer to my inquiry regarding the government's position in the matter of an imperial preference for our apples.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I do not think it is
fair for the hon. member to put it even in that way. I have been very generous to hon. members who have taken part in the discussion of the various items which have been considered in the course of the day, having allowed a great deal of latitude. It is therefore unfair of the hon. member, both to the Chair and to the committee, to put his explanation in that form.

I shall be happy to put
it in any form you suggest, Mr. Chairman. I am only too delighted to come within the four corners of the rules both in the House and in committee, and if I assure you now that I retract the statement wholly I trust that this assurance will bring back that pleasant smile which we all like to see, and that we shall proceed as agreeably as before. Just a word in reply to the hon. member (Mr. Neill). I do not know who made the explanation to which he has referred, but

Supply-A griculture
certainly the department has facilities for examining basic slag produced in Nova Scotia, and this is the first time I have heard it suggested that anyone had claimed that their analysis was not up to standard or that the effectiveness of the fertilizer had been questioned. It has been tried not only in one locality but in thousands of places, and the explanation which the hon. member says was given is certainly no explanation at all. It is absolutely not in accord with the facts as given to me by the people who used the material.
It is in accord with Hansard of last year or the year before.

I can offer some information, derived at first hand, in regard to this subject. I was a representative of that company under Mr. C. L. Walker in our section of the country for years. Indeed, Mr. Walker has slept in my house a good many times. He stopped sending the fertilizer into our section for the reason that it was no good, as we knew from experience. There is no use taking half an hour to answer the point; it has already been answered.

If the hon. gentleman
(Mr. McMillan) will look into the question he will discover how wide of the mark he is. The duty of the Department of Agriculture, in view of this very vote we are now discussing, should be to see to it, by means of a registration system and a method of inspection throughout the whole of Canada, that the goods sold to the farmers of the country are up to the mark and in accordance with the analyses which should appear either on the bag itself containing the article, or on the tag appended to that bag. The information which the Department of Agriculture issues throughout the country should be supplemented by the efforts of men such as my hon. friend representing firms trading in Canada, and more particularly outside Canada, in order to make sure that purchasers shall know exactly what they are buying. And if an article is not up to specification the fact should be reported to the department which is to-night asking for this vote for the purpose of continuing this work.
My hon. friend (Mr. Foster) is on solid ground when he tells the House that the fertilizer industry in Canada, from the Atlantic to the Pacific, was imperilled by the action of the government in taking off the duty of ten per cent which had been in force on this commodity. The reason for the damage to the fertilizer industry in Canada was perhaps not so much the fact that the manufacturers
wanted a protection of ten per cent, as the fact that our manufacturing plants being in a large number of cases considerable distances away from the agricultural communities requiring the fertilizer, the cost of transportation made competition impossible with manufacturers nearer at hand. Let me give a concrete illustration. The city of Montreal is a considerable distance away from the Maritime provinces, who are large consumers of fertilizers; the New England states are comparatively close to those provinces. The records show that immediately this ten per cent duty was taken off, the United States product came in. Previous to that time that protection had enabled manufacturers in Canada as far west as Hamilton and Toronto to sell their product to the Maritime provinces, in spite of the freight rate; but as soon as the reduction was made the producers in Hamilton, Toronto and Montreal found themselves unable to compete with the New England states, so that one by one they went out of business. After they had ceased operations the price of fertilizer to consumers in the Maritime provinces, in Ontario and throughout Canada was raised dollar by dollar, until to-day the farmers are paying more per ton for the American product than they had to pay for the Canadian article before the protection was removed.
Another concrete illustration may be drawn from the city of Hamilton. That city is reasonably close to the Niagara peninsula; so is the city of Buffalo. And in the city of Buffalo such tremendous plants as the Crocker, the Millsom and the Buffalo Fertilizer works, and some four or five other large enterprises find it advantageous to dump their surplus manufactures into Canada after first supplying the home trade. When that ten per cent duty was in force it was sufficient to prevent this dumping, especially in that very large consuming area in the Niagara peninsula. With a slight protection of ten per cent the manufacturers in Hamilton, Toronto and other centres of production in Ontario were in a position to supply the Niagara peninsula, but today we find lying idle in Hamilton a plant capable of manufacturing 10,000 tons of fertilizer per annum and which is waiting for any bidder who wants to acquire any portion of it. It went out of business immediately upon the removal of the ten per cent duty. Take the Swift Canadian Company, which is a large manufacturing concern in Toronto. Originally they were engaged in the city of Toronto in the manufacture of fertilizers from the by-products produced in that city, but they have found it not to their advantage to
Supply-A griculture

continue the manufacture of fertilizers there, and to-day, although they are selling the same brands from Toronto, where are those brands being manufactured? They are made in their plants across the line, and then shipped into the Niagara peninsula. They go through the same avenues of sale as they did previously, but the point of origin is no longer the city of Toronto, but rather the factories which they control and operate in the United States of America.
One hon. gentleman to-night raised a point which is worthy of note, namely, that the most expensive constituent in the fertilizers which are necessary to recuperate the soils of Canada is nitrogen. It will be interesting for this committee to know that according to the report on fertilizers issued by the department, and to which the hon. member for Kingston referred a moment ago, nitrogenous products, which are the base, and the expensive base, used in the manufacture of complete fertilizers in Canada, have been exported from this country since the duty was taken off-mark you, they were exported previously, but not to quite the same extent-to the amount of 29,500,000 pounds last year. That 29,500,000 pounds of nitrogenous product is sufficient base, and expensive base, to manufacture complete fertilizers to the amount of 90,000,000 pounds. That 29,500,000 pounds of raw product was exported from this country largely to that great fertilizer centre in the United States, Baltimore, to be made up there into complete fertilizers, and to a degree shipped back to the consumers in Canada. That represents $500,000 that the manufacturer of this nitrogenous product received for his product from the Baltimore broker or buyer. If that base instead of being shipped in a raw, coarse state largely to Baltimore had been worked up into complete fertilizers in this country-and everybody in this House knows that this country does need in a great many parts complete fertilizers to carry on intensified farming operations-it would have brought to the manufacturers of that product, to the labourers and all who were engaged in its production, the sum of $900,000.

Did the hon. member say
that Canada exported the amount he stated of nitrogen?
Of nitrogenous products.
In what shape?

In the shape of a tankage which would analyse on the average 6 per cent of nitrogen and 20 per cent of bone
TMr. Harris.]
phosphate of lime. One ton of that tankage, containing 6 per cent of nitrogen, 20 per cent of bone phosphate of 'lime, together with sufficient potash added to make up a grade such. as 2.82 fertilizer, would make up three tons of complete fertilizer which our farmers would buy.

Will the hon. member not
admit that the main source of nitrogen is obtained from nitrate of soda, which is produced in Chili and brought up here-imported, not exported?

That is one source, but not the main source. If the hon. member will allow me to go one step further, I say that we exported 'last year 29,500,000 pounds of nitrogenous products, products indigenous to this country and gathered in this country. Would it not be better, instead of allowing those by-products to go to waste by the abattoirs in this countiy, to manufacture them into complete fertilizers, rather than to continue this extravagant importation and the displacement of that business in this country by that extravagant importation? If that industry is going to be put out of business in this country, it is time that we replaced that little 10 per cent duty which was on previously, and which permitted us to overcome the handicap of the freight rates which are so hard on us, due to the fact that the point of origin is far from the point of consumption. Let us again get back to the position where we shall manufacture sufficient complete fertilizers to meet the demands of this countiy in order that we may not only do business among ourselves, but save as well these by-products which are going to waste by the hundreds of tons in all the large centres of population, and which could be turned into a product which our farmers would be glad to buy from us. If the duty were replaced, it would revive this industry, which is indigenous to this country, being so closely allied to agriculture, which everyone knows is our basic industry.

My hon. friend from Toronto-Scarborough has taken us into the question of soil fertility and soil cultivation. When he begins to tell us that the tankage from slaughter houses is the great basis for nitrogen, I would like him to realize that in any successful system of agriculture it is not to that source that farmers look for nitrogen, but to the atmosphere, where we find a composition containing 80 per cent free nitrogen. Those who have been trying to operate their farms to the best advantage realize that the best encouragement we can give agriculture
to grow *uch crops that we are able to get

Supply-Agriculture
that nitrogen, from the air upon terms which are actually better than getting it for nothing, and that is through the growing of alfalfa, sweet clover, peas, beans and that sort of crop. It is all right for my hon. friend, from his point of view, to talk in the manner he does, but we have found as a result of many years' experience, so far as our immediate section is concerned, that so long as we can get the potash and the phosphoric acid, and along with it so much lime, we can get nitrogen very much cheaper than we can buy it in the shape of artificial fertilizer purchased from the factory at a high price.

My hon. friend will agree that it is much easier to get that nitrogen from the air if the soil is in good condition, and that the soil can be brought into that condition much more quickly by the application of commercial fertilizers. The argument advanced by the hon. member '(Mr. Harris) is borne out by the trade returns of Canada for the year 1925. These show that the year before the duty was removed from commercial fertilizers not a pound of nitrate of soda was imported from Chili, whereas last year the importations amounted to 17,270,274 pounds. It is quite apparent to everyone who uses commercial fertilizers on their farms that the price did go down for a few months until it served the purpose of those who secured control, but the price to-day is higher than it was before. Having put the industries almost completely out of business in this country to-day the prices are fixed at Baltimore for the factories which are still operating in Canada. There are still a few of them in operation here but the prices are fixed for them by those who are in the business at Baltimore. The Baltimore people realize it will not be to their advantage to have every one of these fertilizer factories closed, because that would very probably induce the government of Canada to reimpose the tariff against American fertilizers. They still allow a number of factories therefore, to do business in Canada, provided they are allowed to fix the prices, and the Canadian factories do not enter into competition with those engaged in the industry on the other side. I think this is one of the clearest examples of the folly of the course which is being pursued by the present government. Those people who had invested money in this industry in Canada have seen their business in the main destroyed and transferred across the line, and Canadians are at the mercy of a bigger combine than they ever dreamed of. In addition they are paying much more for fertilizers. If the minister will look at the trade returns he will find that the arguments advanced by my hon. friend (Mr. Harris) are borne out to the very letter.

In my opinion the duty on fertilizers did not do either the manufacturer or the agriculturist any good. According to the admission of the two last speakers to my right, the industries for whose benefit the duty was intended have gone to pieces. Before that stage had been reached their product had become too dear for the Canadian agriculturist to use in the manner he desired. One of the largest users of fertilizers in the Maritime provinces, as well as one of the largest potato growers, was the gentleman who sat in the last parliament for Carleton-Victoria, Mr. Caldwell. When this subject was under discussion in 1922, Mr. Caldwell pointed out, as will be found by reference to page 3140 of revised Hansard, June 17, that while we collected a little over $50,000 during the last six years from the duty on fertilizers, the manufacturers charged the Canadian consumer some $3,800,000 extra on account of the duty. Mr. Caldwell was complaining at the time that the cost of raising potatoes was too high. He went on to say that with the exception of acid phosphates the materials entering into the manufacture of fertilizers were free. He said he wanted the duty reduced to five per cent, and added:
There would be little loss of revenue on this account either; we collected less than $90,000 a year during the last six years, but we have paid to the manufacturers or mixers over half a million dollars per year on the material they brought in flee. They are able to charge us this year $9 more than is paid by the farmers in Maine for the same product. Last year the difference was $15.
So we see that while we have kept that spoon-fed industry going for some years in our midst the other industries that were dependent on it have been killed. The tariff on fertilizers has proved a failure, and has been detrimental to the general good of the nation.
What is the price today?

Just a word or two in
reply to the hon. member for South Huron (Mr. McMillan) that hon. gentleman seemed to think he had absolutely closed the entire case by saying that the reason this basic slag company had gone out of business was because their product was of no use, and he stated that he himself knew that because he had handled the product. I merely wish to point out that not merely is the hon. gentleman misinformed, but that if he were to repeat the statement elsewhere it would be characterised
Supply-Agriculture

in language far from parliamentary. The fact remains that the price to the Canadian consumer of fertilizer has risen from S3 to $5 more than it was, in fact the price has become so high that, these manufacturers are able to compete, and are coming back into the market with their product. This conclusively shows that the reduction of the duty put them out of business and produced conditions with which they were unable to compete. However, since the price is returning to the original figure they are opening up their manufacturing establishments again. An hon. gentleman near me disputes this statement, but I am informed that the facts are as I have stated.
Oh, oh.

Some of my hon. friends
are rather amused. Let me tell them that if they investigate the subject they will find that undoubtedly prices have been raised to the consumers and a number of factories have gone out of business.

Please give us some
figures showing those prices.

I should be very glad to
do so, but I did not realize that this question was coming up to-night and therefore did not have the necessary figures available. I promise my hon. friend, however, that I shall be prepared to accommodate him on the first occasion that offers.
I challenge 3rou to prove it.

Why does not my hon
friend, if he is so anxious to get figures, ask the minister to give the desired information? Surely this is information to which the House is entitled.

If the minister does not
want to give the information let me tell the committee that in the little town of Fergus, situated 70 or 80 miles north of Toronto, at the time the duty was taken off acid phosphate, 80,000 pounds of fertilizer a year were bought through a co-operative society. At that time they paid as low as $16 a ton but the best price they could get this year was $20.80 per ton.
Surely the minister in charge of this matter ought to be able to give some information as to the prices for feritilizer in Canada this year compared with last year and previous years.

I was going to make the suggestion that we might be able to get from the Seed branch the prices of these

fertilizers for some years before the duty was taken off-I think that occurred in 1924-as compared with the relative prices at the present time. We do not happen to have that information, and I admit it would be interesting. Up to the present we have not had any necessity for using this fertilizer on the plains of the west For that reason, I suppose, our western friends, including myself, have not made the same study of the subject that eastern members have. But it certainly is news to us all that the way to get cheap fertilizers is to tax them.
'You are propounding a truth nevertheless.

I am always ready to sit at the feet of any eastern Gamaliel on this or on any other question and learn, but I often read of this matter before I had the privilege of being in parliament. There has been an agitation for fertilizers for certain crops, and there has been an agitation by farmers for certain classes of fertilizers. My hon. friends opposite take the ground now that the way to develop eastern agriculture- it is not yet applicable to the plains; it may be some day, possibly-is to tlx the fertilizer which the farmer purchases for his land. If that is true, I have to throw up my hands and say I do not know anything about this subject.
Hear, hear.
Perhaps the minister would refer it to the tariff advisory board.
I was going to suggest that we might refer it to them.
Would the minister allow me a question in regard to binder twine? Perhaps he knows about that.
Yes.

How does that
compare with the price before the duty was removed?

I am afraid I will have to assume charge of another department as well as Agriculture before I deal with all these problems. But the best I can suggest is that this be dealt with before the advisory board, and I think that it will be all right. I am not joking about this.
It is a question of price as compared with the duty.

Will the hon.
member permit a question?

Supply-Agriculture

The minister has those prices; he publishes them every week over his own signature and sends them to me, yet he says he does not know anything about it because he lives on the plains where they do not know anything about fertilizers.
Not this kind.
No, not this kind, but the kind the minister distributes all over the west. I am pointing out that the minister every week publishes the prices of fertilizers, so that he knows them quite well.
Excuse me, I do not.

I followed his pamphlets week after week, and only a few short weeks after the duty was taken off, in his own pamphlet he showed that to the Canadian consumer it was higher all the time. But the result was that put the Canadian competitor out of business and put the American competitor in control. He had his Saskatchewan friends laughing because he said he was removing the tax on fertilizer. Of course if the minister is able to arouse enthusiasm in Saskatchewan by saying that every time you tax you raise the price, it is no tribute to his Saskatchewan followers. But how can you reconcile that with the fact that throughout the country Canadian competition is eliminated and the Canadian consumer pays the price dictated by the American manufacturer? The minister looks helplessly on and says he knows nothing about the subject.

That is another
matter. I did not say I did not know anything about it, but if the way to promote eastern agriculture is to tax fertilizers, then I said I knew nothing about it, and I admit that right now.

Then why do you tax
fertilizers?
That is a different matter.

It does not matter what you call it. You cannot change 'it by giving it a different name. You cannot deceive a clear brain by a phrase or a delusion. We know that the taking off of the tax affected the price in Canada because it eliminated competition. You cannot get around that fact You may get a laugh from those who know nothing about fertilizers, but you cannot ignore the solid facts. They never collide; they are always in harmony. Here we are in this country, with at least hundreds of our workmen gone, producing our goods in the
United States, and the Canadian consumer is paying out of his own pocket for the folly of the minister.
Does the right hon. member, contend that by taking off the tariff you raise the prices of goods?
We do not have to contend; we simply have to show the facts as they exist. If the hon. member cannot see the facts, there 'is no hope of his understanding the argument.

You admit that
is a fact?
What?
You contend that if the tariff is taken off the prices immediately rise?
We contend it and we know it, because we see the facts.

Was that the
only factor entering into the raise? There might be another factor operating.

If you will read the
quotations from Baltimore as given by the hon. member for East York last session you will see that while the prices of goods rose in Canada the prices in the world market fell. In Baltimore, the centre of the fertilizer industry, prices were dropping, while in Canada they were rising.

What would
prevent a Canadian from bringing in these goods free of duty and selling them at the lower price?
He could bring them in if he paid the price dictated by the American manufacturer.
The right hon. member stated that the prices had fallen in Baltimore and in the world market.
There have been many such cases all through the history of tariffs-
Is the hon.member going to answer my question?

There have been many cases where the raising of the tariff has lowered the price. In the United States after they raised the tariff in 1861 they lowered the price on every line of goods manufactured in that country. The prices came down. Not only that, but since the war, when the British government put a tariff on a number of goods on which they had no tariff before, the prices of those goods came down in England, according to statements of Stanley Baldwin, the
Supply-Agriculture

Prime Minister. They have established industries which never existed before, but they have lowered the prices by putting up the tariff. It has been explained by hon. members on this side of the House that they have thus given a market to their own producers, and by producing on a large scale they have lowered the prices.
Does the hon. member contend that the manufacturers in England did not take advantage of the tariff protection given to them?
No, I contend they took advantage of the protection given to them to keep the market to themselves, and lowered the prices to the people of England.
I do not think the hon. member understood my question. I want to know if the manufacturer reduced his price below the level the tariff protection would have given him?

Absolutely. As soon as they got the market to themselves, so that they could purchase on a large scale-just as large production all over the world gives lower costs-they sold goods cheaper to the people. That is the statement of Mr. Stanley Baldwin. I can quote it, and I will do so later.
The hon. member will admit that the manufacturers of England are different from those in Canada.

No, I will not admit that. I say the protective policy of Canada gives the manufacturers in Canada, and the farmers for that matter, an opportunity to hold the market for themselves; and they sell the goods cheaper when they can hold the market for themselves. That is what protection does. That is the mistake my hon. friends from the west make. If you take off the tariff you raise the prices of goods.

I am trying to
answer the hon. member's question.
I was going to ask the hon. gentleman (Mr. McLean), over there- he is a farmer-is it not true-
Let us come back to the item.

My hon. friend had better discuss it in the House rather than go to Montreal and cast a lot of insults on members of this House as he did recently in a speech there. My hon. friend has a good deal more courage among his friends in the city of Montreal than he has in the House of Commons.

Will the hon. member
mention one of the insults?

I can mention many of them; I saw them in the Montreal papers. I was going to ask my hon. friend a question if I am permitted. Not necessarily.
He certainly can, and he can make money by doing so. The manufacturer does the same thing. By keeping the market to himself he cuts down the price to the consumer and gives work to Canadians.

Will the hon.
member tell us then, or will the small town lawyer to his right tell us-

Prior to the time that the duty was removed from fertilizers we had in the harbour of Halifax a fertilizer factory which gave employment to a large number of men, as well as to stevedores and others in connection with handling the raw material that was

Supply-Agriculture
brought there to be manufactured. The duty was removed from fertilizers and the result was that the factory was closed. Those employed in the factory have been scattered. I cannot tell where; probably with many hundreds, many thousands of others, they have crossed the line and are now earning their living in the United States. Instead of this factory being in operation and a considerable sum of money being distributed in wages and in various other ways in my constituency, the factory is boarded up, and as we pick up our daily papers we find columns of advertising matter offering to farmers and other users of fertilizers in our country, Belgian and German fertilizers no cheaper than the home product.
They are better.
I am not prepared to say anything about that.
I am.

Probably they are no better. At any rate the production of that material in my constituency has been stopped, and instead of labour being employed there and money circulating in various ways in connection with that factory, it is closed up and we are importing from Europe Belgian and German fertilizers manufactured by cheap labour while our own people are deprived of emplos'ment in that connection. That is the situation as regards the one factory that I know about, and it is an example of many others throughout our province. They are not so large as many of the western factories and do not give as much employment or pay out as much money, but one after another is being closed up. This is a very serious matter to the people of Nova Scotia and it is one of the grievances we have in that end of the country.

The item before the committee is a rather involved one:
Seed, feed and fertilizer control, including grants to seed fairs, etc.
You might say it consists of four subjects in one and I suppose that has something to do with the wide range the discussion has taken. What proportion of this appropriation of $305,000 will go for salaries and expenses of officials? I notice from the last Auditor General's report an amount of $166,344 was spent for that purpose. Perhaps the minister can give the committee some idea as to the amount for salaries and expenses in connection with the control of the distribution of seed, feed and fertilizers under this item.

The same staff
handles the three services.

In
view of the fact that the fertilizer business has been practically put out of business in this country I would imagine that instead of an increase in the estimate a reduction would follow.
It is largely to keep tab on importations that the inspection staff is required.

I
am afraid the minister is keeping a little too much tab on things and not doing enough to encourage industry in this country. Only on Saturday I went into a place of business in the town where I live and complaint was made as to the number of government officials coming in, forcing them to make returns to the government that are absolutely useless, worrying people into making statements. Some of these people have to keep an extra staff in order to make out statements to the government. They have inspectors coming in, one looking after one particular business, coming in one day and on the following day another one looking after something else, when they might very well be combined. I notice from the Civil Service Commission report a few days ago that about twenty new officials are being taken into the department. There has been a tremendous increase in the staff of the Department of Agriculture since the minister took office. He certainly has not reduced expenses in that respect, and instead of combining four different subjects into one item the minister ought to give us an idea of how much of this vote is being devoted to each of them.

My hon. friend
never misses an opportunity of discussing the number of inspectors we require and the grievance that he holds against the Department of Agriculture because of their number. I took advantage of the opportunity of making a week-end visit to my hon. friend's district a few days ago, As we went through the town of Ingersoll I looked out to see if there was anything exceptional with respect to imported cheese.

Of
course the minister noticed along the river three factories, every one of which was closed down ?

We went on into
Middlesex and spent the week-end there. I did not hear in that district any of these
Supply-Agriculture

complaints, not one. They were in the middle of the sugar-making season, and maybe that was the reason they felt pleasant and did not retail any of the perennial grievances of my hon. friend; but I was looking for them. The people did not seem to show by their vote the other day that they were aggrieved. Did the Minister of Justice hear any complaints while he was up there?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No, not -a word.

I ask the hon.
member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Tobin), did he hear any grievances of this kind?

I
have no doubt that the Minister of Justice was investigating those complaints when his train pulled out and left him!

I have not heard
one whisper of these grievances.

You have no time to
listen to them.
' Maybe not. But what about the vote registered there the other day?
What about the vote registered on the 29th of October in every section of Ontario?

Well, what about
it?

Was there any Peace
River agent there?

Did any pfficer
that the government is responsible for go wrong in any respect in Peace River? The returning officer did not go wrong; it was a deputy.
Oh, I see.

Now, I have really forgotten what the hon. member for South Oxford (Mr. Sutherland) wanted to know. But I can make a pretty straight guess at it- something about inspectors. This work unavoidably and inevitably is largely inspec-tional. In order to keep down the very expense that my hon. friend is complaining about, the same staff administers seed, feed, and fertilizers; consequently the particulars are not kept separately.

Do
any of these inspectors go across the line and inspect the fertilizer plants?
No.

The tariff was referred to as a tax. Now surely the minister will not contend that commercial

fertilizers are not higher in price to-day than they were before the tariff was removed? I think he had better let this item stand until he obtains for the House the exact prices of fertilizers.

I am able now to
give the information asked for by some hon'. members with respect to the number of fertilizer firms that were established and operating last year in Canada. We were nine below the number. We estimated the total at fifty; we have fifty-nine in operation. There were two hundred and eighty-nine registrations of fertilizers.
What is the capacity of those plants?
I do not know.
The minister will realize that these firms are not manufacturing fertilizers, they are merely mixing the ingredients, and the prices are fixed at Baltimore in every instance.

A great many
farmers are doing the mixing for themselves

1
suppose among the fifty-nine are included some farmers who are mixing their fertilizers on the barn floor.
No.

A few years ago during
the war Professor McLennan of Toronto University reported that there were millions and millions of dollars worth of pure nitrogen gas escaping daily into the air. I think he was referring to the Okanagan Valley. That potential wealth is pretty hard to estimate. Has the minister's department, in view of the fact that this country is likely to use a large amount of fertilizer in the future, ever considered doing anything towards utilizing that vast potential wealth?
We have done nothing in connection with it because we do not know where it is located.

Might I recall to the minister's mind that the report was made by Professor McLennan, professor of physics in the University of Toronto, who rendered distinguished service during the war? I think he devised the plan that enabled the British Admiralty to close the straits of Dover to German submarines; and he discovered helium gas. In fact, he is one of the greatest scientists on this continent. People thought the gas was of no use because it would not burn. Surely the minister is alive to the immense potential wealth of this gas?

Acting Ministers
Surely.
Has his department considered taking any-steps to utilize the gas?

I will do so if my
hon. friend will tell me where it is located.
I refer the minister to Professor McLennan, who discovered it.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons

Mr. Chairman, it was understood that this item should stand until the minister obtained the prices of fertilizers.

Item agreed to.

Mr. Chairman, we have
had rather a busy day with agriculture ever since three o'clock, and as it is now after eleven I think we might stop at this point. We have made fairly good progress and have had a very interesting and delightful discussion.

My hon. friend
